column4: This passage opens a direct two-path parallel: the one who gives and is mindful follows the charitable ascent that the section sets against refusing the passage.
The giver's affirmation of the good completes the first path's stance, corresponding to the section's faith and mutual counsel alongside mercy.
The giver is made at ease for ease; this explicitly casts moral choice as a way made passable, echoing the section's guided ways and difficult ascent.
The opposite person is miserly and thinks himself self-sufficient, directly meeting the section's wealthy man who assumes he cannot be overcome.
The second path rejects the good, a specific counterpart to refusing the section's passage of release and feeding.
The withholding person is made at ease for hardship, turning the section's unentered uphill path toward its opposite outcome.
The ayah says wealth will not avail its owner at the fall, a direct outcome for the self-assured spender whose wealth the section links to vanished power.
The declaration that guidance belongs to God meets the section's two guided ways and contrasts guidance with human claims of control.
The warning of a blazing fire gives the rejected path the same fiery endpoint that the section contrasts with a fire used as a guide.
This ayah specifies who enters that fire, helping define the boundary between the two sides of the section's image.
The fire-bound person is described as denying and turning away, a compact parallel to the section's deniers of signs who refuse the passage.
The other path is kept away from the fire, giving the section's right-side people a clear counterpart to its fire-enclosed side.
The God-conscious person gives wealth to purify himself, directly joining the section's spending, care for the poor, and upward moral movement.
The gift is not repayment for a favor owed, clarifying a motive opposite the section's display for people to see.
The giver seeks the face of the Most High Lord, specifying the inward audience that replaces the section's ostentatious giving for people.
The closing assurance of satisfaction completes this giving path's outcome, beside the section's right-side destination.
The announced blazing Fire is an explicit counterpart to the section's sealed Fire at the end of the refused way.
The Fire calls those who turned away, a concrete joining of refusal and fiery destination like the section's unentered passage and covered signs.
The same passage identifies the one who gathered wealth and hoarded it, joining refusal of the way to the wealth that the section says cannot save.
The human is described as created anxious, a close formulation of the section's human created amid hardship and its uphill trial.
When hardship touches him, he is impatient, specifying the panic against which the section says sabr on the ascent must hold.
When good reaches him, he withholds it; this concretely reverses the section's feeding of the hungry and release of the bound.
The righteous keep a known share in their wealth, making the section's act of spending for the needy a standing right rather than display.
The next ayah names the share's recipients as the asker and deprived, directly meeting the section's poor and hungry mouth.
Belief in the Day of Recompense supplies the judgmental setting for the wealth-share just named, like the section's right and left outcomes.
Those who fear their Lord's punishment give a specific stance that accords with the section's patience and mercy before its fire boundary.
The declaration that no one is secure from punishment reverses the section's arrogant assumption that no one can overpower him.
The cave companions send one with their silver into the city to obtain food; this next step after 18:18 connects the threshold scene with the section's city and feeding images.
Abraham asks for this city to be made secure and its people supplied with fruits, a concrete parallel to the section's city fed from hunger and protected from fear.
Abraham settles descendants by the Sacred House in a barren valley and asks for provision; it joins the section's city, lineage, and need for food in one scene.
The secure sanctuary stands amid people seized around it; this supplies another specific city-and-safety formulation beside the section's city fed and made secure.
The oath by the secure city repeats the section's opening oath on the city, adding security as the city's stated quality.
The next ayah says the human was created in the best form, adding a human-creation formulation to the section's created person and faculties.
The human can be brought to the lowest low, a direct vertical reversal of the section's ascent and its person who clings to earth.
Believers who do good deeds are excepted and receive an unfailing reward, specifying how the descent is reversed by the section's charitable way.
This closing ayah explicitly joins faith and good works with mutual counsel to truth and patience, repeating one of the section's named acts and its collective form.
The command to lower the wing of humility out of mercy to one's parents gives an exact downward motion for the section's claim that ascent comes by stooping in compassion.
Severing kinship ties is condemned, a specific reversal of the section's community that pities one another as though from one womb.
Hearing, sight, and heart are each accountable, connecting the section's gifted faculties and the illusion of being unseen to judgment for their use.
On the Day of Witness, tongues and hands testify to what people did; this makes the section's given tongue and its hidden actions publicly answerable.
Mouths are sealed while hands speak and feet testify, turning the section's fear of being unseen into bodily evidence at judgment.
Hearing, sight, and skins testify against their owners, a specific answer to the section's person who thinks no one sees him.
Those who consume orphan property unjustly are promised fire in their bellies and a blaze, joining the section's orphan, wealth, and fiery consequence in one warning.

This command joins protecting orphan wealth, giving full measure, speaking justly even about kin, and fulfilling a covenant; it gathers the section's orphan, measure, relation, and oath motifs in one ayah.
The command not to approach an orphan's property except rightly, followed by fulfilling covenants, joins the section's vulnerable orphan with its oath-bound moral responsibility.
The ayah says that if people mix their affairs with orphans, they are their brothers; this makes explicit the kin-like bond behind the section's orphan and same-womb compassion.
The answer about what to spend names parents, near kin, orphans, needy people, and travelers, directly collecting the section's relational beneficiaries into a giving scene.
The command to give the near relative, needy person, and traveler their due makes the section's kinship and feeding acts concrete duties.
This command lists parents, kin, orphan, needy, neighbor, traveler, and those in bondage as recipients of good treatment, closely matching the section's web of care and release.
The helpers prefer others over themselves even when in need and are protected from miserliness, giving a specific communal counterpart to the section's feeding and mutual mercy.
The person given his record in the right hand receives an easy account, a judgment counterpart to the section's right-side company.
The person given his record from behind his back meets the section's left-side boundary in a contrasting judgment image.
The next ayah says that he will enter a blazing fire, completing the fire consequence of the preceding back-handed record.
Those who spend without following their gift with reminders or injury receive a reward; this neighboring passage supplies the ethical opposite of the section's showy spending.
A kind word and pardon are better than charity followed by injury, sharpening the section's contrast between public display and actual mercy.
Secret charity is better, though open charity is also good; this directly answers the section's spend-for-people-to-see image.
Those who spend by night and day, privately and publicly, receive reward and fear no grief; it gives a specific faithful counterpart to ostentatious spending.
The ayah says righteousness is not reached until one spends what one loves, making expenditure a threshold to goodness like the section's passage.
Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend in God's way face painful punishment, directly tying withheld wealth to the section's refusal and fire.
The hoarded metal is heated in the Fire and used to brand foreheads, sides, and backs, giving a bodily fire consequence to the section's wealth-and-fire conjunction.
The hand is pictured chained to the neck for miserliness and then overextended in spending; this meets the section's neck-release image and the boast of having spent much wealth.
The faithful neither spend extravagantly nor withhold but keep a middle course, a specific counterpoint to the boast of lavish spending without mercy.
The abundant provision makes a person claim honor, opening the same sequence that corrects him for failing to honor the orphan.
When provision is restricted the person claims humiliation; this clarifies the section's hunger and counters treating material measure as a person's worth.
The same people consume inheritance greedily, a specific misuse of wealth against the orphan and kinship that the section calls into mercy.
The gatherer of wealth is cast into the Crusher, beginning a punishment sequence that ends in the shut Fire linked by the section to its closing image.
This ayah asks what the Crusher is, extending the same wealth-and-fire warning toward its explicit fire description.
The Crusher is described as God's kindled fire, a neighboring specification of the fire shut over people in 104:8.
The fire reaches the hearts, adding its inward effect to the closed-fire scene the section links with denied signs.
The expiation for accidental killing includes freeing a believing neck, a separate legal setting that repeats the section's concrete act of releasing a neck.
The ayah warns not to use oaths as a barrier to righteousness, piety, or making peace; it makes the section's oath-and-passage meeting explicit.
The Creator is said to have created everything and determined it with exact measure, another direct creation-and-measure formulation behind the section's sequence.
Everything is created according to measure, a repeated formulation for the section's measurement motif and the human claim about power.
Deeds are weighed, connecting the section's measure/capacity language to the judgment that sorts people by what they have done.
The next ayah gives the heavy-scale person a pleasing life, completing one measured outcome beside the section's right-side company.
The light-scale person supplies the opposite result to the section's right-side path.
The next ayah names the light-scale person's destination as the abyss, completing the adverse measured outcome.
This ayah asks what the abyss is, continuing the measured-judgment scene.
The abyss is specified as a blazing fire, joining measured deeds to the section's fire-bound side.
Those whose scales are heavy are successful; this makes measure determine an outcome like the section's division into right and left companies.
Those whose scales are light lose themselves and remain in Hell, completing the contrary measured outcome with a fire destination.
Anyone who has done an atom's weight of good will see it, directly countering the section's assumption that no one sees and making small deeds visible.
The same rule makes even an atom's weight of evil visible, giving the section's unseen person an exact boundary at judgment.
